snp5.7:2.1: “Nothingness” here is the dimension of nothingness, one of the four formless absorptions, reached (after surmounting the dimension of the infinitude of consciousness) by focusing on the perception “there is nothing.” MN 26 says Āḷāra Kālāma, the Bodhisatta’s first teacher, had mastered this level and took it to be the highest attainment; the Bodhisatta left him on realizing it wasn’t true liberation. Even so, the dimension of nothingness can serve as a basis for the insight that does lead to liberation — see Sn 5:14 (snp5.15) and AN 9:36 below, and on using the formless attainments to cross the flood more generally, see MN 52, MN 106, MN 111, and AN 9:36.
snp5.7:5.4: Following the Thai edition’s bhavetha viññāṇaṁ tathāvidhassa (“would the consciousness of one of that sort be”), reading tathāvidhassa as a fusion of tathāvidhaṁ (“of that sort”) and assa (“his”). The Burmese and Sri Lankan editions instead read cavetha (“would fall/die”) for bhavetha (“would be”); tathāvidhassa could also be read as a straightforward genitive, which combined with cavetha would give “Would the consciousness of such a one fall?”
snp5.7:6.3: For more on this image in light of early Buddhist theories of fire, see The Mind Like Fire Unbound, chapter 1.
snp5.7:6.4: “Name-body” (nāma-kāya) refers to mental activities of every sort.
snp5.7:8.1: On what “criterion” means here, see The Mind Like Fire Unbound, chapter 1; on the Tathāgata as indescribable more generally, see Skill in Questions, chapter 8 and appendix 4.
snp5.7:8.3: Following the Sri Lankan edition’s vajjā (“he/one would say”) over the Thai’s irregular vajju or the Burmese’s vajjaṁ (“they would say”); vajjā fits the meter better, nothing in the dialogue up to this point suggests a “they,” and the parallel line at SN 1:20 also reads vajjā in the major editions. Read as “one would say,” the Buddha’s answer addresses how such a person would appear to an outside observer; read as “he would say,” it addresses how the person would describe his own experience. Either way, there’s no standpoint — from within or without — from which one could rightly say the person doesn’t exist, or that he exists eternally free from disease.
snp5.7:8.4: This is one of the passages where unbinding is treated not as a phenomenon (dhamma) in its own right but as the ending of phenomena; see AN 3:137, note 1.
